data.metric: exact index under contract-specified lowest-index tie rule

evidence.summary: Kernel returns the HIGHEST tied index, not the lowest. Case A (fp16 explicit ties): kernel [2,3,3,2] vs contract-required lowest-index [1,0,3,0] — wrong on all 3 tied rows. Case B (4096x8 coarsely quantized fp16 logits): 1174 rows had ties; mismatches vs lowest-index rule = 1174 (100% of tied rows), mismatches vs highest-index rule = 0, and selected value always equaled the row max. So the kernel computes a correct max value but the exactly-inverted tie-break, matching the `v >= best` source defect.

rationale: Line 17 uses >= rather than >; with a sequential scan over e, >= makes equal values replace the current best, selecting the last (largest) tied index.

scope_evidence.summary: Contract: on ties for the largest logit the LOWEST expert index must win; ties are described as a normal occurrence due to reduced-precision logits.

scope_rationale: The problem statement explicitly makes the tie rule part of the contract: "When several experts share the largest logit, the contract requires the LOWEST expert index to win". It also states ties are routine in reduced-precision router logits, so tied inputs are within the declared domain.
statement: On ties for the maximum logit, _route_kernel uses `v >= best` so a later (higher-index) expert overwrites the incumbent, returning the HIGHEST tied index instead of the contract-required LOWEST index.
